spatial_entity.notes: Historical region broadly corresponding to parts of modern northern Afghanistan and adjacent Central Asia. The documentary corpus spans changing political control; the claim is regional rather than attributed wholesale to any one Sasanian, Kidarite, Hephthalite, Turkic or early Islamic polity.

claim.date_text_original: Bactrian documentary corpus, fourth to eighth centuries CE
claim.summary: Bactrian legal documents from late antique northern Afghanistan directly attest legally recognized slavery. Specialist analysis identifies slaves born in an owner's possession and slaves purchased for money, treatment of enslaved people as personal property, manumission by payment of the slave's price, and sale of children into slavery during hardship. A surviving deed from 700 CE transfers a female slave together with an estate. This supports P3 institutional slavery for the documented Bactrian region while avoiding attribution of uniform practice to each successive ruling empire.

territorial_practice.notes: P3 rests on court-produced legal documentation of slave status, purchase, property treatment, manumission and family sale, plus a surviving deed transferring an enslaved woman. It remains below P4 because documentary legal visibility does not quantify demographic prevalence across all of Bactria or across the full four-century interval.

source.title: Slavery Represented in Bactrian Documents
source.independence_notes: Dedicated specialist study of slavery using the Bactrian documentary corpus and Nicholas Sims-Williams's editions/translations.
source.reliability_limitations: The surviving documents are uneven in place and date and legal documentation cannot by itself measure population-wide prevalence.
